newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Reforms needed to propel Bangladesh market.
newsitem.headline: Reforms needed to propel Bangladesh market.

text.p: Bangladesh's securities market, dogged by price manipulation charges and lack of transparency, needs overhauling to restore investor confidence, analysts said on Monday.
They said the main Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE), a money-spinner for investors on the floor and in the unofficial kerb market late last year, had gone into virtual hibernation.
Share prices rocketed for four months before the bubble burst and scared off small investors.

"Timely action (by authorities) would have saved the situation and protected the interest of a large number of investors," Moazzem Hossain, editor of the daily Financial Express, told Reuters on Monday.
He said reforms in the DSE and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), computerised trading, and separation of trading from management could restore investor confidence.
A SEC inquiry in December after stock prices started falling sharply following the four-month rally found dozens of brokers and companies were involved in price manipulation.

But Hossain said the SEC was too slow to act. "The SEC should be manned in its key positions by people professionally competent and having no conflict of interest either real or perceived in both primary and secondary markets," he said.

The stock market started to rally soon after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina took power following an election in June 1996. The DSE benchmark index shot up from below 1,000 to more than 3,600 in the first week of October.

The SEC, the stock market watchdog, imposed circuit breakers or caps on price movements in November to stabilise the market and warned against trading in 24 companies with poor financial track records.
Investors in the kerb market reacted angrily, staging protests outside the exchange building and clashing with police.
Hossain said a central depository system should be introduced for transparency in trading and state-owned companies privatised to raise market liquidity.
"The government must give credible signals through its action that there will be transparency in all operations of the market," he said.
Abu Ahmed, a Dhaka University professor of economics, said he favoured a neutral DSE Council.
"The council members should not be involved in trading to ensure transparency of transactions," he said.
Ahmed proposed that the DSE's membership be increased to 300 from the present 195.
Moreover, companies should be barred from selling their shares within one year of completion of their projects, he said.
"There must be stricter rules and all loopholes plugged through reforms. Without this the confidence of the investors will not be restored."
Ahmed also suggested foreign audit firms be allowed to operate in the country to earn the confidence of foreign investors and attract overseas capital into the market.
He said the government should expedite the launching of the proposed national stock exchange "to create a competitive environment".
SEC Chairman Haroonur Rashid said on Monday the government had already launched an awareness programme to educate investors about how to operate in the stock market.
"The regulatory framework is being reviewed and strengthened for smooth running of the capital market," he told Reuters.
